03 / 08 Data cleaning · Trusting the numbers

Before we can trust the data, we have to clean it.

  • 21,597 King County house sales, 2014–2015
  • 4 columns had missing values
  • 177 duplicate listings found
Result
28.6% of rows needed correction

waterfront, view, sqft_basement and yr_renovated accounted for every gap. The 177 duplicates turned out to be genuine resales of the same house — not data errors — so we kept the most recent sale of each.

Before cleaning After cleaning Still open (waterfront)
04 / 08 Hypothesis 1 · "Waterfront"
Hypothesis 1

"Waterfront homes sell for roughly 30% more than comparable homes."

Result
Confirmed — and then some

Comparing homes of the same grade, waterfront properties cost between +36.8% (grade 7) and +102.5% (grade 11) more than non-waterfront homes of that grade.

No waterfront Waterfront (incl. hidden)
05 / 08 Hypothesis 2 · "Average age"
Hypothesis 2

"Waterfront homes are, on average, about 20 years older than other homes."

Result
Not confirmed

Confirmed waterfront homes are older — +8.8 years (52.7 vs. 43.9) — but not by 20. And the hidden waterfront homes we found (see slide 07) break the pattern entirely: they're −9.0 years younger than average (34.9).

06 / 08 Hypothesis 3 · "City located"
Hypothesis 3

"Waterfront, renovated, high-grade homes are the most expensive segment — ~80% sit near cities or large lakes."

Result
Not confirmed

Of the 13 homes matching all three criteria (waterfront, renovated, grade ≥ 9), 100% sit outside the four major cities we checked — this segment is a rural / lakeside premium, not an urban one.

Waterfront · renovated · grade ≥ 9 (size = price) Major city
07 / 08 Best insight · Hidden waterfronts

Waterfront houses are missing.

A GIS distance join between every house and King County's real water-body geometry revealed 125 "hidden" waterfront homes — sitting within 25m of water, but never flagged as waterfront in the original listing data. That nearly doubles the known waterfront inventory: 146 → 271.
